title: Indian Army's 20-Member CWG Squad Delivered 16 Medals and 41 Percent of India's Tally
excerpt: All four Army women boxers won gold in Glasgow as the military's Mission Olympics programme proved its case for institutional backing of elite sport.
body:
• The Indian Army sent 20 athletes to CWG 2026 Glasgow and returned with 16 medals — eight gold, seven silver, and one bronze — accounting for 41% of India's total haul.
  • All four Army women boxers — Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, and Arundhati Choudhary — won gold, a clean sweep across 51 kg to 70 kg categories.
  • The four women are Corps of Military Police recruits who joined under the Agnipath scheme, training at the Army Sports Institute in Pune through the Mission Olympics programme.
  • Beyond boxing, Army athletes claimed gold in judo, para athletics, and medals across weightlifting, athletics, and javelin — Neeraj Chopra added silver as an honorary Lieutenant Colonel.

The Indian Army's 20-member contingent at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow returned with 16 medals — eight gold, seven silver, and one bronze. The count represents 41% of India's total tally of 39 medals across the entire Games, according to figures released by the Army on August 2.

The headline belonged to boxing. Eleven Army boxers competed in Glasgow; eight won medals, finishing with six gold and two silver. Most striking was the women's squad: all four Army women who entered the ring left with gold around their necks.

Four Women, Four Golds, One Programme

Naib Subedar Preeti Pawar (54 kg), Naib Subedar Jaismine Lamboria (57 kg), Havildar Sakshi Chaudhary (51 kg), and Havildar Arundhati Choudhary (70 kg) each topped their categories to complete a sweep across the 51 kg to 70 kg range. All four serve in the Corps of Military Police, recruited as sportspersons after the Agnipath scheme opened rank-and-file enlistment to women.

"Inside the ring we fight for our countries. Outside the ring we are friends."

— Jaismine Lamboria, after beating defending champion Michaela Walsh of Northern Ireland

Jaismine arrived in Glasgow as the reigning 57 kg world champion from Liverpool 2025 and had already received the Sena Medal in January 2026. Sakshi's gold required a weight-class gamble: she dropped from 54 kg to 51 kg on coaches' advice, beat two-time world champion Nikhat Zareen and reigning 48 kg world champion Minakshi Hooda in national trials, then ended England teenager Ruby White's 68-fight winning streak in the final.

Arundhati knocked out defending champion Rosie Eccles of Wales in the semi-final before a unanimous-cards final win over England's Chantelle Reid. She joined the Army in 2022 as a direct-entry Havildar under the Mission Olympic Programme, having recovered from a head injury that hospitalised her for a month and later from wrist surgery. Preeti Pawar, an Asian Games bronze medallist, opened India's boxing gold rush with a unanimous win over Canada's Scarlett Delgado and became the first woman athlete directly inducted as a Junior Commissioned Officer, according to the Army.

Beyond the Ring: Medals Across Six Sports

The Army's medal run extended across five sports beyond boxing. Harsh Singh won gold in the men's 60 kg judo — one of India's first two CWG judo golds alongside Asmita Dey. Soman Rana took gold in the men's F57 shot put, with Shubham Juyal completing an Indian 1-2 for silver.

Gulveer Singh delivered a historic double, winning silver in the 10,000 m and bronze in the 5,000 m to become the first Indian track and field athlete to win two individual medals at a single Commonwealth Games. Sarvesh Anil Kushare of the Regiment of Artillery took India's first CWG silver in the men's high jump. Weightlifter Valluri Ajaya Babu set a Games snatch record of 149 kg. Neeraj Chopra, who holds an honorary rank of Lieutenant Colonel in the Territorial Army, added a javelin silver to the Army's count.

How Mission Olympics Built the Pipeline

Mission Olympics is the Indian Army's talent identification and training scheme for elite sport. Selected athletes train at the Army Sports Institute in Pune, run in collaboration with the Sports Authority of India. The practical effect is straightforward: an athlete receives a salary, a rank, and full-time access to coaching, physiotherapy, and competition without needing outside sponsorship.

For young women from small towns, the programme removes the financial argument families often use against a sporting career. Three of the four women boxing gold medallists — Preeti, Jaismine, and Sakshi — are from Bhiwani in Haryana, the town that produced Olympic medallists Vijender Singh and Akhil Kumar. Arundhati is from Rajasthan but trained in Bhiwani before moving to the Pune institute.

What Glasgow Sets Up Next

Jaismine Lamboria carried the Indian flag at the closing ceremony, where the Commonwealth Flag was handed to India ahead of Ahmedabad hosting the 2030 Games. India finished fourth in the medal table with 13 gold, 17 silver, and nine bronze — boxing alone contributing seven of those golds, more than any country has ever won in the sport at a single CWG edition.

With the Asian Games approaching, the depth the Army's quartet has shown in the 51 kg to 70 kg range gives Indian boxing a settled core to build on. Eight of India's 13 golds in Glasgow were won by women, and the Army's institutional model — salary, rank, training infrastructure — offers a template that federations relying on ad hoc sponsorship rarely match.
nri_angle: The Army's Mission Olympics model offers a replicable institutional path for Indian athletes abroad and those watching from the diaspora who follow India's evolving sporting infrastructure.
